messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

At fifty-four, Ingrid had spent thirty years commanding her kitchen with quiet authority, but that authority had been shattered nine months ago when a male sous-chef she had personally mentored assaulted her in the walk‑in cooler. She could not find the words to describe what happened—the memory arrived as jagged fragments: the click of the latch, the cold steel shelving pressing into her back, the crushing weight of his body pinning her in the same position she now finds herself in whenever the memory surfaces. That visceral bodily reenactment was the only language her memory spoke, and it left her wordless, unable to narrate the event even to herself. What she could articulate was the betrayal. She had trusted him, trained him; his attack had rewired her understanding of the world: people cannot be trusted, you never know who will harm you. Now, certain conversations—a coworker’s offhand comment about loyalty, an earnest compliment from a regular customer—made her stomach turn. When a male server lingered too long at her station, her throat tightened. Emotional closeness, whether from a concerned friend or a warm exchange with a line cook, felt like a setup for another betrayal. Each time someone stepped too close or a conversation veered toward intimacy, the fragmented images of the cooler flooded back—the metal, the weight—and each time, the memory hardened her belief that she was foolish to have trusted anyone. Because she now lived with the conviction that harm could come from anyone, Ingrid had become hypervigilant. She startled at the sudden movement of a waiter’s hand reaching for a plate. Strangers approaching the kitchen entrance made her breath catch as though they were coming for her. These startle responses themselves triggered the fragmented memories, and each wave of fear confirmed that her distrust was justified—the world was indeed dangerous. Her mistrust had also reshaped what she noticed: she now scanned conversations for hidden menace, which meant that even ordinary topics like a coworker’s marriage troubles became triggers for her. Her constant alertness meant that she was acutely aware of every man who entered her vicinity, making male presence a near-constant trigger. The recurring intrusive memory, with its wordless reenactment, was a relentless reminder of her vulnerability, deepening her sense of betrayal with each recurrence. The conviction that she should have seen it coming kept pulling her back into the memory, as if her own failure had locked the door behind her. She had begun delegating the closing duties to her female sous‑chef, never staying late alone. Her husband, Tomas, noticed she had stopped inviting friends over, and their own conversations had grown stilted as she avoided any topic that felt too personal. What brought her to the clinic was a panic attack during a dinner service when a male customer reached across the counter to thank her. She had frozen, her body locked into that same position, and had to be led from the kitchen. She is afraid that she will never be able to work again, but more than that, she is terrified of the person she has become—someone who sees a threat in every friendly gesture.
